extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and newspaper editors (readers of Associated Press wartime dispatches)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and presentation conventions for daily wartime newspaper dispatches: short datelined items, agency attribution, vivid frontline detail, official communiqués, bylines and concise headlines aimed at general readers. Covers multi-topic front-page reporting during World War II-era conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and location attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Items begin with a city and date dateline like "LONDON, Feb. 3—(AP)" or "Cairo, Feb. 3" to show where and when the dispatch originated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include city and date at the start of each dispatch; when distributed by an agency, indicate it (e.g., "(AP)") immediately after the dateline so readers know the report's provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source attribution and agency tagging
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories consistently attribute information to sources such as "Associated Press", broadcasts ("a Cairo broadcast heard in London"), foreign newspapers ("a Swiss newspaper said"), official communiqués and named correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always identify the originating agency, broadcast, newspaper, correspondent or official communiqué for claims and reports; when quoting radio/broadcast items or foreign press, state how the dispatch was heard or received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise headline summarizing the main event
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent headlines succinctly state the primary fact or action, e.g., "Pope Refuses to Leave Rome Despite Pressure from Nazis" and "YANKS BREAK INTO CASSINO, THEN RETIRE".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a short, attention-getting headline that encapsulates the core news action or development; headlines should be factual and reflect the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate lead paragraph with key facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads present the essential facts up front (who, what, where, when) — for example, opening lines describing German notification to the Pope, Allied troops reaching Cassino, or the Spanish Cabinet's neutrality policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the most newsworthy facts in the first paragraph so readers quickly grasp the situation; follow with attribution and supporting detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quotations and identified speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports include direct quotes and identify speakers and roles (e.g., Lt. John Murphy of Philadelphia; Msgr. Fulton J. Sheen; Gen. George C. Marshall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include verbatim quotes to convey eyewitness voice or official stance, and name the speaker with a brief identifier (rank, title, city) to establish credibility and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of battlefield detail and human-interest anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispatches mix operational details (positions, counterattacks, artillery, tank movements) with human vignettes and casualty incidents (e.g., medical men with red crosses, individual soldiers’ experiences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance strategic/military facts with vivid, on-the-ground anecdotes to humanize the story and give readers a sense of events' immediacy and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of official statements and communiqués
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories quote or summarize official communications such as government communiqués, cabinet policies, radio broadcasts, or Allied communiqués (e.g., Spanish Cabinet ratified neutrality; Vatican radio broadcast recorded by Associated Press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an official statement is available, report its content and provenance; indicate whether the text is a communique, broadcast, or ministerial statement and attribute it clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of numerical reporting and casualty/force figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles include numeric details and estimates (casualties, prisoner counts, troop movements, bomber counts) such as "3,000 Nazi casualties", "100 prisoners", or "more than 2,000 American bombers".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numbers where available but attribute estimates and be transparent about uncertainty or source; use figures to quantify scale and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bylines and correspondent identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces carry bylines or correspondent credits (e.g., "By HAL BOYLE", "By ROBERT VERMILLION", "Associated Press Correspondent") indicating who filed the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include bylines for feature/dispatch pieces and identify the correspondent and their location to lend accountability and authorial voice to the report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple short dispatches and topic-stacked front page
rubrics_metrics.description: The page presents many short, discrete dispatches on varied topics (Pope/Vatican, Spain neutrality, Cassino fighting, shipbuilding, diplomatic protests) arranged as separate datelined items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize front-page content as distinct datelined blocks for each development so readers can scan multiple concurrent stories; use subheads and spacing to separate items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corroboration and cross-sourcing (radio, newspapers, dispatches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports often corroborate information by referencing different channels (e.g., "A dispatch to The London News Chronicle supported the same idea" or "a Cairo broadcast heard in London declared...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm important claims by citing multiple independent sources when possible (radio, foreign press, official communiqués); report the degree of confirmation when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation notices and page referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer items or related stories include continuation markers or page references (e.g., "Page 2", "See...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an item continues beyond the front snippet provide clear page references or continuation cues so readers can find the full report.
